newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS-Strong magazine paper ops in UPM H1.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Strong magazine paper ops in UPM H1.

text.p: Europe's largest forestry group UPM-Kymmene on Thursday said disposals boosted first half earnings, but analysts said operating profits were also good, and magazine papers a strong surprise.

UPM said profit before extraordinary items and tax rose 70 percent to 3.53 billion markka from 2.08 billion in the year-ago period, with over two billion markka of gains from divestments booked at the operating level.
That included a large chunk of shares in compatriot telecoms group Nokia Oy.
"If you look at the operating level, virtually all business areas were better than we had expected," said Aros Securities analyst Carl-Henrik Freijborg.
UPM said that excluding the gains from asset sales, second quarter operating profit on ongoing businesses was 11 percent of turnover, up from eight percent in Q1.

The overall January-June result was at the top end of analysts' forecasts in a 3.15-3.57 billion markka range, but UPM's stock fell on a weak Helsinki bourse, trading down 2.50 markka at 139.50 at 1100 GMT.
Net sales were flat at 26.42 billion markka against 26.17 billion, with earnings per share up sharply at 10.20 markka from 6.17 markka in the year-ago period.
But a UPM statement noted a decline in profitability in the first half, due to lower prevailing prices than in 1996, when they were still relatively high.
"Despite a significant increase in the volume of sales, profitability excluding gains from asset sales was weaker than for the first six months of last year," the statement said.
Analysts said the magazine paper unit had been especially positive, almost doubling its operating profit in Q2 to 201 million markka from 144 in Q1, helped by the stonger dollar.
"That was a positive surprise," said Merita Securities analyst Pertti Aaltonen.
UPM said it expected full-year earnings, excluding gains from asset sales, to be about the same as last year when it posted a 3.56 billion markka profit before extraordinary items.
CEO Juha Niemela told Reuters Financial Television that he expected the trend of improving quarterly earnings to continue.
"What is important is that this last quarter was clearly better than the quarter before, so we have already three consecutive quarters towards the better, and we expect that to continue," he said.
Strong demand and a rise in pulp prices would gradually pave the way for higher paper prices, but magazine and newsprint prices would be lower than in the second half of 1996, UPM said.

Analysts are still mixed on forestry shares, but some have turned more positive this month as rising pulp prices feed hopes for higher paper prices. UPM's earnings did not change some already positive recommendations, although forecasts would be upgraded on the better-than-expected figures, they said.

Looking ahead, the trend in pulp prices -- up 13 percent last week at $583.2 per tonne from their lowest point this cycle in mid-April, according to the Finnish options exchange SOP's pulp price index -- and fine paper prices would be key.
Many fine paper producers plan price hikes around 10 percent but with one new machine in Europe due for start-up in November, there is still uncertainty about the plans, Aaltonen said.
"Clients usually react to start-ups in advance," he added.

Freijborg said pulp producers' stocks -- a key factor for the price -- which rose in July by some 125,000 to 130,000 tonnes -- would rise again in August, but ought to stabilise or fall again in September to support higher prices.
"September will be very important," he said.
